title: Pray differently
hook: pray not "let me get this" but "let me not crave it," not "let me be rid of it" but "let me not fear" (Meditations 9.40)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was rushing river, and Marcus asking only that the smallest thing move forward. Your line was the smallest thing.

Late at night, the asking comes. Let the test come back clear. Let me get the job. Let this pain go away. Let my kid be okay. People of every faith, and people of none, find themselves sending wishes like these out into the dark. Marcus did too. Near the end of book nine he wrote a short reflection on his own prayers, and it turns the asking around.
screen: `LATE AT NIGHT, THE ASKING.` → `LET THIS PASS.` → `PRAY DIFFERENTLY.`

segments.voice: Either the gods have power or they don't, Marcus writes. If they don't, why pray at all? If they do, why not pray for the power not to fear these things, not to crave them, not to grieve over them, rather than praying only that they come or don't come? Someone might say: the gods put that in my own power. Then, Marcus answers, isn't it better to use what's in your power with freedom than to strain like a slave after what isn't? And who told you the gods don't help us even with what's in our power? Then his examples. One person prays: how can I win that woman? You: how can I stop wanting to? Another: how can I be rid of this? You: how can I stop needing to be rid of it? Another: how can I not lose my little son? You: how can I not be afraid to lose him? Turn your prayers this way, he says, and see what comes. Read him fairly. Marcus is writing to himself, a Stoic, about his own prayers, not anyone else's. People in many traditions pray for healing and for their children, and many also pray for courage and peace in the same breath. And the little son is not abstract. Marcus and his wife Faustina lost a number of their children young.
screen: `EITHER THE GODS CAN, OR THEY CAN'T.` · `USE WHAT'S IN YOUR POWER, FREELY.` · `NOT LOSE HIM, OR NOT FEAR LOSING HIM.` · `HIS OWN PRAYERS, NO ONE ELSE'S.` · then, large: `LET ME NOT FEAR.`

segments.voice: Name one wish you've been carrying, and hold it honestly; you don't have to give it up. Underneath it, notice the fear or the craving that comes with it. If you pray, you might bring both, the wish and the calm, in whatever words your own tradition gives you; if you don't, simply hold the turn: less fear of this.
Pray differently. Marcus's turn: not only let me get this, but let me not crave it; not only save me from this, but let me not fear it. Today's word.
Your line: let me not fear. The wish can stay; the fear can loosen. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 612 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WILL YOU EVER BE GOOD?`

options: how can I not lose him?

original.note: Greek: I pray, I ask, I wish. Marcus's turn changes what the asking is for.

trapdoor: what you thought: a philosopher dismissing prayer.
what it means: Marcus keeps praying, but asks for freedom from fear and craving, not only for the outcome.
what a scholar hears: the entry is a short dilemma argument, either the gods can act or they can't, a form Marcus uses again and again in the Meditations.

chat.says: Did Marcus Aurelius think praying was pointless?
options: No. He turned his prayers from 'spare me this' toward 'let me not fear it.'
Yes. He said the gods have no power, so prayer is wasted breath.
No. He said pray only for outcomes, since feelings are ours to fix.
chat.meaning: In 9.40 Marcus asks why not pray not to fear, crave or grieve, rather than only for outcomes. He's writing about his own prayers.

Faustina.meaning: Marcus's wife; several of their children died young

Stoic.meaning: the Greek and Roman philosophy Marcus followed

Marcus.meaning: Marcus Aurelius, Roman emperor who wrote the Meditations

notes: 9.40 paraphrased, including the three examples (the woman, being rid of something, the little son) and 'Turn thy prayers this way, and see what comes' (Long). Confirm.
